report.releaseDate: 22 Oct 2026 (Receita Federal Sept-2026 collection data); framed by MP 1.394 of 25 Sep 2026
report.currency: BRL (R$) primary; ~USD alongside at USD/BRL 5.37. Tables in R$ bn unless stated.
report.verdict: Brazil's regulated fixed-odds market was running at a record ~R$3.3–3.5bn (~$0.62–0.65bn) of monthly GGR and had already delivered R$11.1bn (~$2.07bn) of federal betting-and-lottery receipts in nine months when the Lula government switched it off: MP 1.394/2026 banned all sports betting and online gaming from 25 Sep 2026, forced platforms dark on 6 Oct and extinguished every authorisation on 25 Oct with no refund of the R$30m (~$5.6m) fee. January–September 2026 is therefore the high-water mark of a 21-month regulated experiment; whether a legal market returns — and in what shape — now rests on STF Justice Fux and a Congress that must act before the measure lapses around March 2027.
summary: **The market was switched off at its peak.** Provisional Measure (MP) 1.394/2026, signed 25 Sep 2026 — nine days before the first-round election — prohibits the operation, offer, intermediation and advertising of all fixed-odds betting (sports and online games) nationwide, including offshore supply to persons in Brazil. Deposits stopped on publication, sites and apps went dark at 00:00 on 6 Oct, and every federal, state and district authorisation was extinguished 30 days after publication (25 Oct) with no refund of the outorga and no indemnity (MP art. 4).

**Size: a ~R$40bn-a-year market.** SPA data obtained under the access-to-information law (LAI) put regulated fixed-odds GGR at R$20.07bn (~$3.74bn) in H1-26, +15.3% on H1-25 (R$17.4bn / ~$3.24bn), after R$36.96bn (~$6.88bn) in FY-25, the first regulated year. Monthly average was R$3.35bn (~$624m); January peaked at R$4.29bn (~$799m), Feb–Mar fell to ~R$2.8bn (~$521m), and June — 19 World Cup days, 72 matches — was only R$3.34bn (~$622m): no tournament spike.

**Stakes and payout.** Prizes returned to bettors in H1-26 were R$377.86bn (~$70.4bn), implying stakes of ≈R$398bn (~$74bn) and a payout ratio of ≈95% [estimate from SPA figures]. A separate SPA-sourced report puts H1-26 deposits at R$88.48bn (~$16.5bn) and GGR at R$20.28bn (~$3.78bn) — a 1% gap to the BNLData figure; GGR equated to ~23% of deposits.

**Online-only market; product split not disclosed.** Regulated fixed-odds in Brazil is in practice 100% digital (there is no meaningful licensed retail sportsbook estate); retail gaming is the Caixa lottery monopoly plus state lotteries. SPA does not publish a verified sports-vs-online-games GGR split — n/a.

**Player base: 30.9m CPFs, modest growth.** 30,895,934 unique CPFs had bet on licensed sites by end-H1-26 (cumulative since Jan-25), +9.8% on 28.1m; average spend per bettor rose 5.0% to R$649.60 (~$121) per semester (R$108.27 / ~$20 a month). 68.5% male; 72% aged 40 or under; only 2.8% over 60.

**>5m Brazilians were already barred.** Minister Durigan (13 Aug 2026): ~3m Bolsa Família/BPC beneficiaries (banned since Oct-25), 1.2m self-excluded and ~0.8m Novo Desenrola debt-renegotiation participants could not bet — a structural brake on volume growth.

**Licensing regime (as it stood).** Law 14.790/2023: federal authorisation at R$30m (~$5.6m) for five years and up to three brands, Brazilian-incorporated entity, SIGAP reporting, monthly fiscalisation fee (aggregate ≈R$115.2m/~$21m a year per the government's own impact note). Operators grew from 78 companies/182 brands (H1-25) to 87/188 (H1-26, +11.5%/+3.3%). All pending applications are voided (MP art. 6).

**Tax regime: GGR-based, ratcheting.** Operators paid a 12% contribution on GGR (destinations: sport, tourism, public security, health, education), raised by Complementary Law 224/2025 (26 Dec 2025) to 13% in 2026, 14% in 2027 and 15% from 2028 — the extra 1–3pp earmarked for social security — plus ordinary IRPJ, CSLL, PIS and COFINS. Bettors pay 15% income tax on net prizes above the first IRPF exemption band. H1-26 legal allocations of R$2.49bn (~$464m) equal 12.4% of GGR.

**Tax take: 9M-26 already beat FY-25.** Receita Federal (22 Oct 2026): betting and Caixa-lottery federal receipts were R$11.116bn (~$2.07bn) Jan–Sep 2026 vs R$9.95bn (~$1.85bn) for all of 2025. September was R$1.206bn (~$225m), +3.7% m/m but -7.9% y/y (R$1.310bn / ~$244m Sep-25). Fixed-odds alone generated R$6.86bn (~$1.28bn): R$3.72bn (~$693m) in statutory allocations and R$3.14bn (~$585m) in federal taxes. [Press-relayed; Receita report not opened directly.]

**Who got the money.** Of H1-26 allocations, sport took R$870.15m (~$162m) via the Ministry of Sport and state secretariats; health R$24.19m (~$4.5m) funding the SUS gambling-harm programme (telehealth from March 2026, Sírio-Libanês contract R$2.94m / ~$548k). Receita's specific codes also show lotteries contributing R$4.96bn (~$924m) in H1 vs R$2.48bn (~$462m) from fixed-odds, Mega-Sena-type numerical lotteries being 77.2% of the lottery block.

**Government's own fiscal cost of the ban is R$12bn over three years.** EM 2114/2026 books lost tax revenue of R$1.541bn (~$287m) in 2026, R$5.150bn (~$959m) in 2027 and R$5.330bn (~$993m) in 2028, plus R$268.8m (~$50m) of lost fiscalisation fees; it claims no outorga loss because fees were pre-paid. BNLData's counter-estimate at H1-26 run-rates is ≈R$18.2bn (~$3.39bn) foregone Oct-26–Dec-27 vs the government's R$6.8bn (~$1.27bn).

**Wind-down mechanics are punitive and payments-led.** Operators faced R$200k (~$37k) daily fines for refund failures; banks/PSPs had seven days to return balances to the CPF-matched account of origin, with residuals swept to a Caixa escrow from 15 Oct; banks, payment institutions and Pix arrangement owners are barred from processing any fixed-odds transaction (art. 14) and the BCB must build a real-time rejection/return protocol (art. 15). App stores, OS vendors and platforms carry a duty of care, with fines up to 10% of Brazilian group revenue capped at R$50m (~$9.3m) per infraction.

**Advertising goes from restricted to prohibited.** Pre-ban rules (Law 14.790 bonus ban; SPA Portaria 1.231/2024 on minors, 'easy money' claims and warnings) are replaced by a blanket ban on all communication, marketing and sponsorship (art. 16), with a 10-day removal deadline; breaches are 'abusive advertising' under the Consumer Code with counter-advertising sanctions.

**Politics: the ban survived the election.** Lula was re-elected on 25 Oct 2026 against Flávio Bolsonaro, whose camp criticised the shutdown but favours a sports-only regime with online casino banned. The government (SRI minister José Guimarães, 27–28 Oct) lists the MP among its three legislative priorities and wants a vote before year-end, before a more conservative Congress sits in Feb-27. As of 27 Oct no joint committee had been installed and 99 amendments were on file.

**Judiciary: no relief in force.** ADIs 8.024, 8.027 and 8.028 sit with Justice Fux, who deferred until after the runoff and has now convened a public hearing with 26 participants (government, sector, football clubs). Of 19 federal-court actions, none has an injunction in force; a TRF-3 panel dissolved the one favourable first-instance ruling within 24 hours (9 Oct).

**Black market was already large and is now the only market.** LCA/Locomotiva for IBJR estimated 38–44% of online betting in H1-26 was on illegal sites despite SPA blocking >25,000 domains in year one (and >16,000 cited by Vixio). ANJL's Legitbet counts >34,000 clandestine betting sites since the MP. Channelisation, not demand, is the variable the ban has broken.

**Industry damage is already structural.** ANJL: ~51% of the ~15,000 people employed by licensed operators have been laid off or furloughed; football sponsorship income has been severed; player balances have been emptied and the statutory welcome-bonus ban makes re-acquisition expensive. Vixio expects heavy consolidation toward tier-one balance sheets if the market reopens.

**Timeline to clarity runs to Q2-27.** 9 Nov 2026: MP enters 'urgency' (locks the docket); December: possible expedited vote or deferral to the new legislature; ≈4 Mar 2027: 120-legislative-day expiry, which would automatically restore Law 14.790 (Congress would then need a legislative decree to re-validate licences); April 2027: possible vetoes/overrides.

**Read-through for B2Tech.** Brazil's legal TAM is zero until at least Q1-27 and the modal outcome is a narrower sports-only regime at 14% GGR plus corporate tax and heavier payments/advertising controls. Do not commit capital to market access now; keep optionality via B2B/supplier readiness and watch the STF window (Nov) and the December vote. The pre-ban numbers — ~R$40bn (~$7.5bn) annualised GGR, 30.9m players, 95% payout — remain the best evidence of what a restored market is worth.

segments.name: Fixed-odds market: sports betting & online games (Jan–Sep 2026)
segments.headline: A ~R$40bn-a-year online market growing mid-teens, with no World Cup spike, abruptly halted after nine months.
narrative: The Secretariat of Prizes and Bets (SPA/MF) does not publish a regular public statistical bulletin; the hardest numbers for 2026 come from SPA data released under the access-to-information law and reported by BNLData. On that basis regulated fixed-odds GGR was R$20.07bn (~$3.74bn) in H1-26, +15.3% on the R$17.4bn (~$3.24bn) of H1-25, following R$36.96bn (~$6.88bn) in FY-25. The monthly profile is instructive for anyone modelling Brazil: January was the peak at R$4.29bn (~$799m) because state and Brasileirão calendars were pulled forward ahead of the World Cup; February and March fell to roughly R$2.8bn (~$521m); April–June recovered to a ~R$3.3–3.4bn (~$615–635m) range; and June, with 19 World Cup days and 72 matches, produced R$3.34bn (~$622m), slightly below the semester average of R$3.35bn (~$624m). The tournament did not lift GGR — a useful corrective to event-driven forecasts.

Stakes and payout can be inferred rather than read. Prizes paid in H1-26 were R$377.86bn (~$70.4bn), so stakes were ≈R$398bn (~$74bn) and the blended payout ≈95% — a hold of ~5% that is consistent with a casino-heavy product mix, since sportsbook alone would not run that thin. A second SPA-sourced report (via Claudio Dantas, 25 Sep 2026) gives H1-26 deposits of R$88.48bn (~$16.5bn), GGR of R$20.28bn (~$3.78bn) and 84 companies/193 brands; the 1% GGR gap and the different operator counts versus BNLData are unexplained and we quote the LAI figure as primary. GGR at ~23% of deposits points to high recycling of winnings into further play.

The player base is large but no longer expanding fast. 30,895,934 unique CPFs had an active registration by end-H1-26 (cumulative since the market opened in Jan-25), up 2.77m or 9.8% on the 28.1m a year earlier; BNLData's Q1-26 cut showed ~15.2m CPFs actually betting in the quarter with R$7.6bn (~$1.42bn) of gross revenue attributed to 'sports betting' and active accounts +11.7% — we cannot verify whether that R$7.6bn is sports-only or total, and treat the product split as n/a. Average spend per bettor rose 5.0% to R$649.60 (~$121) per semester, i.e. ~R$108 (~$20) a month. Demographics skew young and male: 68.5% men; 21.3% aged ≤24, 22.0% aged 25–30, 29.0% aged 31–40, 17.7% aged 41–50 and under 3% over 60.

Growth was deliberately throttled by exclusion policy. More than 5m Brazilians were barred from licensed platforms by August 2026: ~3m Bolsa Família and BPC beneficiaries (prohibited from October 2025), 1.2m voluntary self-exclusions and ~0.8m participants in the Novo Desenrola debt programme, which imposes a minimum six-month betting block. For an operator this means the regulated addressable base was already ~15% smaller than the registered base and skewed away from the most price-sensitive cohort.

Q3-26 GGR has not been published. Using the R$3.72bn (~$693m) of statutory allocations reported by Receita for Jan–Sep and the 12–13% contribution rate implies 9M GGR of ≈R$29–31bn (~$5.4–5.8bn) and a Q3 run-rate of ≈R$3.2–3.5bn (~$0.6–0.65bn) a month — in line with H1 and consistent with September tax receipts being only mildly dented by the 25 Sep deposit freeze [estimate]. Annualised, the pre-ban market was tracking ~R$40bn (~$7.5bn) of GGR, which would place Brazil among the three or four largest regulated online markets globally. From 6 Oct 2026 regulated GGR is zero; the only 'market' is offshore.

Commercially, the H1 data describe a market that had moved from land-grab to steady state: mid-teens GGR growth, high-single-digit player growth, a 95% payout (i.e. heavy casino and promotional intensity despite the welcome-bonus ban), and 87 licensees fighting for ~R$3.3bn a month — roughly R$38m (~$7m) of GGR per company per month on average, with the long tail far below that. The ban hit before the inevitable consolidation; it will now happen in the dark.

segments.name: Licensing regime and the MP 1.394 wind-down
segments.headline: A R$30m, five-year federal authorisation regime built since 2024 was extinguished in 30 days, with no refund, no indemnity and pending applications voided.
narrative: Until 25 Sep 2026 Brazil ran a federal authorisation (not concession) model under Law 14.790/2023 administered by SPA/MF: a Brazilian-incorporated company paid an outorga of R$30m (~$5.6m) for five years covering up to three brands, operated on a .bet.br domain, reported through the SIGAP system, met technical-certification and AML requirements and paid a monthly fiscalisation fee that the government's own impact statement values at ≈R$115.2m (~$21m) a year across the sector. States and the Federal District could also authorise fixed-odds within their territory. Licensee numbers rose from 78 companies/182 brands in H1-25 to 87/188 in H1-26, with more applications in the queue. The sector employed ~15,000 people directly (ANJL).

MP 1.394/2026, published in an extra edition of the Official Gazette on 25 Sep 2026, prohibits the operation, offer, intermediation and advertising of fixed-odds lotteries 'in physical or virtual form, including by agents based abroad offering to persons located in Brazil' (art. 1), expressly covering both real sporting events and virtual online-game events, while leaving other lottery modalities untouched. Article 2 extends the ban to state and district concessions. Article 4 extinguishes all authorisations 30 days after publication (25 Oct 2026), states that the extinction is 'for reasons of public interest' and confers no right to full or partial refund of the outorga nor to compensation. Article 6 bars new authorisations and voids pending applications. The MP also repeals the operative articles of Law 14.790 (arts. 1–40, 43–48, 54), Chapter V of Law 13.756/2018 and art. 68 of Law 15.421/2026 (the FIFA Women's World Cup 2027 law, which had authorised FIFA-partner fixed-odds offers), while preserving SPA's supervisory and sanctioning powers over past conduct.

The transition schedule was compressed and payments-centric. New deposits were prohibited from 25 Sep; bettors had until 23:59 on 5 Oct to withdraw voluntarily; sites, apps and store listings had to be taken down by 6 Oct on pain of blocking; within two days operators had to prove liquidity for full refunds (including voided open bets and settled prizes) and send CPF-level balance files to their banks and to SPA (art. 8), with a R$200,000 (~$37k) daily fine for non-compliance; banks and payment institutions then had seven days (9–14 Oct) to return funds to the account of origin, and unreturnable balances were swept to a dedicated Caixa Econômica Federal account from 15 Oct (art. 9). Operators remain liable for shortfalls, must keep all records for five years and must keep transmitting SIGAP data on pre-closure activity (arts. 10–11). Pending sanction proceedings are suspended and will be archived if operators comply fully with the wind-down (art. 13) — an amnesty-for-cooperation lever.

Legally the measure is temporary: a provisional measure lapses unless converted into law within 60 + 60 days, extended by recesses — Vixio puts the effective expiry around 4 Mar 2027, with 'urgency' locking the congressional docket from 9 Nov 2026. If the MP lapses or is rejected, Law 14.790 revives automatically and Congress must issue a legislative decree governing acts performed in the interim (i.e., whether the 25 Oct revocations stand and whether operators must re-apply and re-pay R$30m). If it is converted with amendments — 99 were filed by late October — Brazil will have a new statute. The industry is arguing before the STF that there was no constitutional 'urgency' (the market had been regulated for 21 months) and that revocation without compensation breaches acquired rights; the AGU argues the Union has plenary competence over lotteries.

The commercial implication for a prospective entrant is that Brazilian licence value has been repriced to near zero for now, and the credibility of any future authorisation is impaired until either the STF or Congress establishes that pre-paid fees and five-year terms are protected property. Operators who paid R$30m in late 2024/2025 have had 21 of 60 months. Any re-entry decision should assume (a) re-application and possibly a second fee unless Congress waives it, (b) tighter conditions (sports-only is the modal compromise), and (c) a far smaller set of competitors — consolidation among the 87 is now inevitable.

segments.name: Tax & fiscal: GGR contribution, LC 224/2025 ratchet and the 2026 take
segments.headline: Receipts were running ~R$1.2bn a month and had beaten FY-25 by September; the Treasury itself books a R$12bn three-year hole from the ban.
narrative: The operator tax base in Brazil is GGR, not turnover. Law 14.790/2023 set a 12% contribution on gross gaming revenue (stakes less prizes), with statutory destinations across sport, tourism, public security, education and health, on top of ordinary corporate taxation (IRPJ, CSLL, PIS, COFINS) — which, for a presumed-profit or real-profit payer, lifts the effective burden on GGR well into the 20s in percentage terms depending on margin structure. Complementary Law 224/2025, published 26 Dec 2025 to help close the 2026 budget, introduced a ratchet: 13% in 2026 (12% for public policies + 1% for social security), 14% in 2027 (+2%) and 15% from 2028 (+3%). Earlier government attempts to go straight to 18% (MP 1.303/2025) lapsed in Congress; the Senate's CAE had at one point voted 15%/15%/18% before the final 13/14/15 schedule prevailed. Bettors pay 15% income tax on net annual prizes above the first IRPF exemption band, with Receita's ComprovaBet statement introduced for the 2026 filing season under IN 2.299/2025.

The 2026 receipts tell a story of rapid formalisation. Receita Federal's Jan–Apr 2026 series for betting houses showed R$4.586bn (~$854m), +99.1% on R$2.283bn (~$425m) a year earlier, though monthly volatility was high: January R$1.49bn (~$277m), February R$1.04bn (~$194m), March R$859m (~$160m), April R$1.189bn (~$221m). We caution that this series appears to include Caixa lotteries despite being labelled 'apostas esportivas' in press reporting, because it is too large to reconcile with the R$6.86bn (~$1.28bn) of fixed-odds-only receipts for the full nine months. The fixed-odds-specific collection codes tracked by BNLData rose steadily from R$368.4m (~$69m) in January to R$513m (~$96m) in June, totalling R$2.48bn (~$462m) in H1 — almost exactly the R$2.49bn (~$464m) of statutory allocations computed from SPA GGR data (12.4% of GGR), confirming the two datasets capture the same 12% flow and should not be summed. Lottery codes contributed a further R$4.96bn (~$924m) in H1, with a jump in the numerical-lottery contribution code from R$11.6m in January to R$251.1m in June that BNLData attributes to a mid-year rule change (unverified).

The headline nine-month figure released on 22 Oct 2026 is R$11.116bn (~$2.07bn) of federal receipts from betting and lotteries, versus R$9.95bn (~$1.85bn) for all of 2025 — a full-year total surpassed with a quarter to spare. September was R$1.206bn (~$225m), +3.7% on August's R$1.163bn (~$217m) but -7.9% on September 2025's R$1.310bn (~$244m); it was the last month of normal operation, with deposits frozen only from the 25th. Within the 9M total, fixed-odds operators generated R$3.72bn (~$693m) in statutory allocations and R$3.14bn (~$585m) in federal taxes (IRPJ, CSLL, PIS, COFINS), per Receita's forecasting coordinator Marcelo Gomide. BNLData had been forecasting R$14.6–15.5bn (~$2.7–2.9bn) for FY-26; that is now unattainable, and Receita's Claudemir Malaquias has said only the non-fixed-odds lottery stream will continue to report.

The government's own fiscal arithmetic in EM 2114/2026 is modest and, in our view, understated. It books tax losses of R$1.541bn (~$287m) for 2026, R$5.150bn (~$959m) for 2027 and R$5.330bn (~$993m) for 2028 — a run-rate of ~R$430m (~$80m) a month, against observed fixed-odds receipts of ~R$760m (~$142m) a month in 9M-26 — plus fiscalisation-fee losses of R$38.4m (~$7.2m) for Sep–Dec 2026 and R$115.2m (~$21m) a year thereafter (R$268.8m / ~$50m over the triennium). It explicitly claims no loss on outorgas because fees were already paid in full, which is precisely the point operators contest. BNLData's estimate, applying H1-26 run-rates, is ≈R$18.2bn (~$3.39bn) foregone between Oct-26 and Dec-27 against the government's R$6.8bn (~$1.27bn) for the same window, and the EM concedes that transfers to legal beneficiaries will be cut, with 2027–28 adjustments to be sent with the PLOA 2027.

For an operator the tax read-through is twofold. First, any restored Brazilian regime will inherit the LC 224 ratchet (14% in 2027, 15% in 2028) and probably a political premium on top; 18% remains the government's revealed preference. Second, the fiscal dependency created in 21 months — R$870m (~$162m) to sport in one half-year alone, plus club sponsorships — is now the strongest argument the Centrão and the football lobby have for restoration, and the reason Vixio and others rate a permanent, total ban the least likely outcome.

segments.name: Payments, player protection & advertising
segments.headline: A Pix-only, CPF-bound, bonus-free regime that was already the strictest in Latin America has been converted into a payments blockade and a total advertising ban.
narrative: Brazil's regulated model was built on the payments rail. Under Law 14.790 and SPA ordinances, deposits and withdrawals could only move between a CPF-verified bettor account and an operator transactional account held at a BCB-authorised institution in the operator's own name, via Pix, TED or debit; credit cards, cash, boletos and crypto were prohibited, and onboarding required document plus facial-biometric verification. That architecture is what made the shutdown executable in 10 days: the MP's refund mechanism simply reversed the Pix flows to the CPF-matched account of origin, with Caixa as the backstop for anything unmatched. The same architecture is now being turned against the offshore market. Article 14 prohibits banks, payment institutions and the owners of payment arrangements — explicitly including instant payments — from processing, settling or enabling any fixed-odds transaction, obliges arrangement owners to write that prohibition into their rulebooks and to exclude non-compliant participants, and article 15 directs the BCB to build a data-messaging system allowing real-time rejection and interbank return of funds linked to illegal betting. Article 28 further amends Law 14.790 so that funds frozen in accounts of irregular operators can be forfeited to the Union through an administrative process without prior judicial decision, with proceeds to the National Public Security Fund.

Player-protection policy had been tightening through 2025–26 before the ban: beneficiaries of Bolsa Família and BPC were excluded from October 2025 (≈3m people), the self-exclusion register reached 1.2m, and participants in the Novo Desenrola debt-renegotiation programme (~0.8m) were blocked for at least six months. The health system stood up a telehealth gambling-harm service in March 2026, initially 600 consultations a month and expanded under a Proadi-SUS partnership with Hospital Sírio-Libanês (contract R$2.94m / ~$548k), funded from the R$24.19m (~$4.5m) health allocation in H1-26. The government's stated rationale for the ban (EM paras. 3–7) is that these instruments 'have not been capable' of protecting health, consumers, minors and household finances, citing studies that net household transfers to betting platforms 'may have been tens of billions of reais' in 2025 and pointing to 24/7 availability, instant settlement and targeted digital marketing as the drivers.

Advertising moves from restriction to prohibition. The pre-ban framework — SPA Portaria 1.231/2024 (no targeting of minors, no 'easy money' or social-mobility claims, mandatory warnings, Conar self-regulation) and Law 14.790's ban on welcome and advance bonuses — was already restrictive, and the STF had in November 2024 unanimously confirmed Justice Fux's injunction against betting advertising aimed at children and adolescents. MP 1.394 art. 16 now bans all communication, publicity, marketing and sponsorship relating to fixed-odds betting in any physical or digital medium directed at the Brazilian public, regardless of format or remuneration, with a 10-day removal deadline (5 Oct) for physical and digital material and sponsorship signage; art. 17 grandfathers only incidental pre-existing content. Breach is 'abusive advertising' under art. 37 §2 of the Consumer Code, sanctioned through the national consumer-protection system including counter-advertising orders, and internet application providers carry a duty of care to prevent circulation of such content (art. 19), with notice-and-takedown on request of consumer authorities or the Justice Ministry (art. 20).

For an operator the implications are structural rather than cyclical. Even in a restoration scenario, the payments-rail controls and the forfeiture power will remain the enforcement spine, so any grey-market strategy carries acute counterparty and asset-seizure risk; the bonus ban means re-acquisition of a player base whose balances have been zeroed will be expensive and slow; and the advertising environment, if it returns at all, is likely to be closer to the Italian 'Dignity Decree' end of the spectrum than to the pre-2026 Brazilian one.

segments.name: Enforcement, illegal market and the political–judicial path
segments.headline: Offshore supply already held 38–44% before the ban; with Lula re-elected and no injunction in force, the decisive windows are the STF hearing in November and a congressional vote before the March 2027 expiry.
narrative: Enforcement under the regulated regime was active but losing ground. SPA reported more than 25,000 illegal sites blocked in the market's first year (January 2026 release), working through Anatel and CGI.br, and Vixio cites over 16,000 illicit domains blocked; yet the LCA Consultores/Instituto Locomotiva study for IBJR estimated that 38–44% of all online betting in H1-26 still took place on unlicensed platforms. Since the MP, ANJL's Legitbet monitor claims more than 34,000 confirmed clandestine betting sites. Blocking has therefore shifted from protecting a 56–62% legal share to attempting to suppress 100% of a demand that the SPA's own figures put at ~R$3.3bn (~$620m) of GGR a month. The MP's answer is to move the choke-point from DNS to payments (Pix rejection protocol) and to platforms (duty of care for app stores, operating systems and social networks, fines up to 10% of Brazilian group revenue capped at R$50m / ~$9.3m per infraction), coordinated by a new Casa Civil-chaired Interinstitutional Committee with mandatory data-sharing among the Federal Police, Receita and COAF.

The judicial track has produced no relief. Three direct actions of unconstitutionality (ADIs 8.024, 8.027 and 8.028) are before Justice Luiz Fux, who signalled he would rule only after the 25 Oct runoff and has instead convened a public hearing with 26 participants spanning government, the sector and football clubs; the AGU is defending the measure on the basis of the Union's competence over lotteries, while the sector argues absence of constitutional urgency and breach of acquired rights. In the lower courts, a survey on 26 Oct found 19 actions in TRF-1 and TRF-3 with no injunction in force: three denied, one granted and then suspended by TRF-3 within 24 hours (the Stake case, 9 Oct) to avoid 'market distortion', and others pending. Any reopening before 2027 therefore requires a market-wide STF injunction, ideally ex tunc so as to unwind the 25 Oct revocations.

The political track is less favourable to the industry than Vixio's pre-election framing assumed. Lula won the runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro on 25 Oct, so the MP's author is not a lame duck; his campaign had framed the election as a plebiscite on bets, and the government's SRI minister José Guimarães named the MP on 27–28 Oct as one of three legislative priorities alongside the public-security PEC and the 2027 budget, with the explicit aim of voting before the current, more pro-gambling Congress gives way to a more conservative one in February 2027. Against that, the MP had no joint committee installed a month after publication, 99 amendments have been tabled, and the Centrão, clubs and state governments face concrete losses: R$870m (~$162m) to sport in H1-26 alone, federal receipts of ~R$760m (~$142m) a month from fixed-odds, and sponsorship income across Série A. The Bolsonaro camp's declared position — restore sports betting, keep online casino banned — gives the opposition and the Centrão a ready compromise text.

We therefore weight the four scenarios as follows (judgement, not modelled): a sports-only conversion with online games prohibited is the single most likely outcome (we would put it at roughly 40–45%); lapse or rejection with Law 14.790 reviving and a reinstatement decree 25–30%; a permanent total ban 15–20%; and an STF injunction restoring the full market before Congress acts 10–15%. In every scenario except the last, no licensed revenue is possible before Q1-27, and in the sports-only case the restored TAM is materially smaller than the ~R$40bn (~$7.5bn) pre-ban run-rate because the ~95% payout indicates online games carried the majority of GGR. The one certainty is that the regulated operator count will be far below 87 on the other side.

segments.name: Lotteries, retail & land-based
segments.headline: Caixa's lottery monopoly is untouched and is now the only reporting gambling tax stream; land-based casinos remain unlegislated.
narrative: The MP is explicit that 'other lottery modalities authorised by law' are outside the prohibition (art. 1 §2), so the federal lotteries operated by Caixa Econômica Federal — numerical prognostics such as Mega-Sena, Lotofácil and Quina, instant tickets and the sports-prognostic pools — continue, as do state lotteries in the modalities they are authorised to run (their fixed-odds concessions, however, are extinguished under art. 2). Receita's specific collection codes show lotteries contributed R$4.96bn (~$924m) in H1-26, two-thirds of the R$7.44bn (~$1.39bn) captured by betting-and-lottery codes, with numerical lotteries alone 77.2% of the lottery block; Caixa's own sales and prize data for 2026 were not retrieved in this research and are n/a. Receita officials have said this stream will continue to be reported after fixed-odds disappears, which means the published 'apostas e jogos de azar' line from October 2026 onward will be a lottery series and should not be compared with 2025–26 totals.

Retail is therefore Caixa's ~13,000 lottery agencies (count not re-verified) — a distribution network with no legal fixed-odds product and no licensed sportsbook estate, which is why Brazil's regulated fixed-odds market was in practice an online-only market and why the shutdown could be executed through payments and domain blocking alone. The land-based casino, bingo and jogo do bicho legalisation bill (PL 2.234/2022) remains in the Senate with no 2026 vote; the political climate created by the MP makes passage less, not more, likely in the near term, although the ban has revived the Paulo Guedes-era argument for integrated-resort casinos as a 'controlled' alternative.

For B2Tech the lottery segment is closed (federal monopoly; state lotteries procure through concessions and largely as iLottery/instant products), and land-based is a 2028+ question at the earliest. The relevant retail fact is negative: Brazil has no omnichannel hedge, so a Brazilian strategy is entirely a bet on the online framework being restored.

highlights.text: Proven demand at scale: ~R$40bn (~$7.5bn) annualised GGR, 30.9m registered bettors, ≈R$398bn (~$74bn) of H1 stakes and 87 licensees prove Brazil is a top-tier online market the moment legal supply returns — demand is not the risk, channel is.

Automatic reversion path: if Congress neither converts nor rejects MP 1.394 by ≈4 Mar 2027, Law 14.790 revives by operation of the Constitution; a reinstatement decree waiving re-application and the R$30m (~$5.6m) fee is the industry's stated ask and has precedent in Brazilian MP practice.

Sports-only compromise is the modal outcome and would hand surviving sportsbook operators a far less crowded market: the ~95% blended payout implies online games carried most GGR, so a sports-only regime shrinks the TAM but also removes casino-led competitors and lowers regulatory temperature.

Fiscal dependency created in 21 months is the restoration lobby's best weapon: R$11.1bn (~$2.07bn) of 9M receipts, R$870m (~$162m) to sport in one half, club sponsorships and the Treasury's own R$12bn (~$2.2bn) three-year loss estimate all argue against a permanent total ban.

Forced consolidation creates entry-by-acquisition options: ~51% of sector jobs already cut, balances zeroed and 87 licence-holders with 39 months of pre-paid term in limbo mean brands, Brazilian corporate shells and local teams can be acquired at distressed prices ahead of any reopening.

B2B positioning is lower-risk than B2C: suppliers (e.g., Evolution signalling readiness to reopen its Brazil studio) carry no outorga risk and can re-enter on day one of restoration; a platform/content partnership with a tier-one survivor preserves optionality without capital at risk.

lowlights.text: Expropriation without compensation is now precedent: MP art. 4 revokes five-year authorisations after 21 months 'in the public interest' with no refund of the R$30m (~$5.6m) fee and no indemnity; until the STF rules otherwise, Brazilian licence value carries sovereign-risk discounting no regulated peer market requires.

The author of the ban won: Lula's re-election on 25 Oct and the government's decision to prioritise conversion of the MP before Congress turns more conservative in Feb-27 remove the 'lame-duck lapse' scenario; a permanent ban on online games — Bolsonaro's position too — is a live, cross-party outcome.

No judicial relief in force: 19 federal actions, zero injunctions, one granted and dissolved within 24 hours; Fux has opted for a public hearing rather than a ruling. Legal clarity realistically arrives Q1–Q2 2027, implying 5–9 months of zero regulated revenue.

Tax ratchet is locked in regardless of outcome: LC 224/2025 takes the GGR contribution to 14% in 2027 and 15% in 2028 on top of IRPJ/CSLL/PIS/COFINS, and the government's revealed preference (MP 1.303/2025) was 18%; a restored market would face a higher effective rate than the one that produced 2026's numbers.

Black market is now the whole market: 38–44% of online betting was already offshore in H1-26 despite >25,000 blocked domains; Legitbet counts >34,000 clandestine sites since the MP. Re-channelising players who have migrated, with the welcome-bonus ban intact and balances emptied, will be slower and costlier than the 2025 launch.

Payments-rail weaponisation and administrative forfeiture: banks, PSPs and Pix arrangement owners are barred from processing any fixed-odds flow, the BCB must build real-time rejection, and funds in blocked accounts can be forfeited to the Union without a prior court order — grey-market operation in Brazil now carries asset-seizure risk, not just blocking risk.

Data opacity: SPA publishes no regular statistics; market size relies on LAI requests relayed by trade press, two SPA-sourced H1 figures differ by 1% and the product split is unpublished — any Brazilian business case rests on second-hand numbers.

forecast.intro: The bridge from a pre-ban forecast to today runs through a single legislative act. Entering 2026 the regulated market was tracking FY-25 GGR of R$36.96bn (~$6.88bn) toward ~R$40bn (~$7.5bn) on H1-26's +15.3% growth, with BNLData projecting R$14.6–15.5bn (~$2.7–2.9bn) of FY-26 betting-and-lottery receipts and LC 224/2025 lifting the GGR contribution to 13%. MP 1.394/2026 drove regulated GGR to zero from 6 Oct, extinguished all 87 authorisations on 25 Oct and, by the government's own account, removes R$1.541bn (~$287m) of 2026 and R$5.150bn (~$959m) of 2027 tax revenue — figures we and BNLData regard as understating the observed ~R$760m (~$142m) monthly fixed-odds take by roughly half. The moving parts for the next six months are the STF (Fux hearing, November), the congressional calendar (urgency 9 Nov; government push for a December vote; expiry ≈4 Mar 2027) and the content of the 99 amendments, of which the sports-only variant is the pivot.
forecast.view: Our base case is that Brazil does **not** return to its pre-ban shape within the next 12–18 months. We assign roughly 40–45% to Congress converting MP 1.394 with amendments that **restore sports betting and permanently prohibit online games**, most likely voted in the December 2026 window or carried into the new legislature with a similar text; 25–30% to the measure lapsing or being rejected around March 2027 with Law 14.790 reviving and a reinstatement decree; 15–20% to a permanent total ban; and 10–15% to an STF injunction restoring the full market first. In the modal case, 2027 regulated GGR would be an estimated **R$12–18bn (~$2.2–3.4bn)** — our judgement that sports carried roughly 30–45% of pre-ban GGR given the ~95% blended payout, with a 2027 restart lag and re-acquisition friction — taxed at **14% of GGR plus corporate taxes**, with advertising closer to a near-total ban than to the 2025 regime and the payments-rail enforcement machinery kept in place against offshore supply. Operator numbers would fall from 87 toward 20–30 well-capitalised sportsbooks. Leverage on the sector is unambiguously negative: zero revenue, continuing SIGAP and refund obligations, severed sponsorships and litigation costs through at least Q1-27 favour tier-one balance sheets. For B2Tech the recommendation is **no B2C capital commitment before the STF ruling and the congressional text are known**, active monitoring of distressed-asset opportunities, and a B2B/supplier-side readiness plan that can be switched on within one quarter of any reopening. The swing factors are Fux (a market-wide ex tunc injunction would reset everything), whether the Centrão trades casino for sportsbook, and whether the government's December push succeeds before the Congress elected on 4 Oct 2026 takes its seats.
watch: STF: outcome of Justice Fux's public hearing (26 participants) and any plenary ruling on ADIs 8.024/8.027/8.028 — specifically whether relief is market-wide and ex tunc (unwinding the 25 Oct revocations) or prospective only.

Congress: installation of the joint committee, the rapporteur's text among 99 amendments (watch for a sports-only carve-out and a licence-reinstatement/fee-waiver clause), 9 Nov urgency lock, December floor vote vs deferral to February 2027, and the ≈4 Mar 2027 expiry.

BCB regulation under MP arts. 14–15 (Pix rejection/return protocol) and the Casa Civil Interinstitutional Committee's first enforcement actions — the template for post-restoration offshore suppression.

Receita Federal monthly 'apostas e jogos de azar' line from October 2026: how far it falls toward a lottery-only ~R$0.5bn (~$93m) a month, and the PLOA 2027 revisions to beneficiary transfers — the fiscal pain gauge for Congress.
Black-market indicators: Legitbet clandestine-site count, IBJR/LCA channelisation updates, and app-store/social-platform enforcement cases under arts. 19–22.

Industry structure: licensee insolvencies, brand/shell disposals, ANJL/IBJR employment data, and whether tier-one operators (and suppliers such as Evolution) maintain Brazilian entities and staff through the blackout.
Tax trajectory: LC 224/2025 step to 14% on 1 Jan 2027 and any revival of the 18% proposal in the conversion text or the 2027 budget.
